CA-06.001: material remains, oral histories and written records give different kinds of evidence about people in the past. a tool can show manufacturing choices. an oral account can preserve names and relationships. a written account can record transactions, while expressing its author's interests and point of view. fossil and genetic evidence place the origin of homo sapiens in africa. agricultural histories vary by region. archaeologists have evidence for local plant domestication in eastern north america, and clay tablets from ancient mesopotamia document one early writing tradition. these examples answer different historical questions and belong to different regional timelines. spaceflight examples have more precise recorded dates. sputnik 1 became the first artificial satellite to orbit earth in 1957. in 1969 the apollo 11 crew carried out the first human landing on the moon. surviving evidence is unevenly distributed. new findings can change an interpretation, and a few examples cannot represent all historical experiences. archaeology oral history
CA-06.002: institutions are durable patterns of rules and practices that structure social activity. some are formal, with stated rules and roles. others, such as conventions for asking or granting help, persist through shared expectations. practices can differ between regions and change within a community. exchange is one way people distribute goods, services and labor. markets are one form, and gifts and shared obligations are others. the photographed market in onitsha shows one place where people trade. it cannot show the full set of rules or relationships under which they do so. distinguish observed practices from stated ideals and disputed accounts. different participants may describe who benefits or exercises power differently. institution exchange
CA-06.003: fossils preserve parts of past bodies. comparisons of bone shape and geological dating help place them in time. fossils from jebel irhoud in morocco show a combination of older and more recent-looking traits. researchers reported a date of roughly 315,000 years, with a stated uncertainty of 34,000 years, for heated stone artifacts from associated deposits. early homo sapiens lived in africa. evidence from fossils, archaeology and ancestry shows people later spread to other continents. repeated movement, separation and contact shaped human populations. today's shared ancestry and diversity reflect many of these histories. a site dates particular evidence. it does not mark the instant a species began. population history and the times and paths of some migrations remain under investigation. fossil migration
CA-06.004: cultivation and domestication describe different changes. cultivation means people tend plants or growing conditions. domestication involves inherited changes in a population through interaction with people across generations. archaeologists identify some of these changes by comparing preserved plant remains. eastern north america is one region with evidence for local plant domestication. settlements have many forms and may change with seasons, food sources and social ties. at mesa verde, in what is now colorado, ancestral pueblo people farmed land on the mesa tops. changes in the recorded structures show that the landscape held different kinds of settlements over time, including cliff dwellings. cultivating food did not cause every society to follow the same path. surviving plant remains, archaeological sites and community histories give different parts of the record. domestication settlement
CA-06.005: writing uses recurring marks and conventions to represent language. some records begin with practical information about quantities or people. the metropolitan museum of art interprets the clay tablet in the image library as a probable account of barley and emmer wheat. its material helps it survive, and understanding the marks still depends on comparing many records. other writing traditions left different materials and purposes. at yin xu in china, inscriptions on oracle bones are evidence of writing in the late shang period. written documents can preserve evidence of transactions, names or speech. surviving documents reflect particular authors, institutions and conditions of preservation. the oldest surviving evidence of a practice may be younger than the practice itself. written records preserve only part of what people communicated. inscription script
